t: 'God in man' or 'God come in the flesh'?
p: Lake prints 'God in man'; the Greek manuscript and the Latin have 'God come in the flesh'.

readings.w: Lake's text (1912): 'justified by early patristic quotation, and (slightly corrupted) by A' (the Armenian)
Greek manuscript G and the Latin version (L)
readings.en: God come in the flesh (Lake: 'God become incarnate')

why: Lake follows the reading that early church writers quote. Athanasius's Greek has it: in Migne's printing of On the Councils 47 the line reads en anthrōpō theos, 'God in man' (Patrologia Graeca 26, column 776), as the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers English does. In the same quotation Athanasius spells 'born and unborn' differently (see the note on those words). Claude's suggestion, not Lake's: the other reading may be a scribe's change toward the familiar words of 1 John 4:2 ('having come in the flesh').
b: Both readings say that Christ is God and truly human. 'God in man' fits the pattern of the verse, where each line is a pair of short opposites (flesh and spirit, born and unborn, death and life). 'God come in the flesh' (Greek en sarki genomenos theos) names the event, God becoming flesh, in words close to 1 John 4:2 and John 1:14: 'And the Word became flesh' (John 1:14). Either way the line answers the false teachers of 7:1, who denied that Christ was truly human.
